value: no significant effect of urban noise (about 65 dB) versus forest-noise control (about 45 dB) on calling when noise was tested in isolation (without urban light)
eye: ear; calling behaviour of wild-caught males under noise playback
method: two nights of one-hour chorus/rival/silence playback loops in single-male enclosures; four treatments (Control, Noise, Light, Light + Noise) with call number, rate, overlap, complexity and amplitude scored
conditions: Wild-caught male tungara frogs (80 collected at six urban and seven forest sites around Panama City, 45 called in the set-up) housed individually in the lab at STRI Gamboa for at most five nights, September and October 2019, then released at their capture sites. Noise treatments: urban noise about 65 dB versus forest noise about 45 dB 'at the center of the enclosure, SPL meter; A weighted, fast, and low' (so the stimulus level is stated at the frog's enclosure centre); reference not stated. Treatments: forest light and forest noise (Control, 13 calling frogs), forest light and urban noise (Noise, 9), urban light and forest noise (Light, 11), urban light and urban noise (Light + Noise, 12); frogs from forest (23) and urban (22) origin. The control is forest-noise playback, not silence; one baseline night with no playbacks preceded two treatment nights. The noise-alone null is a statement about noise tested in isolation; other effects in the same paper involve light: urban light raised peak-to-peak amplitude by 4.7 dB during chorus playback (p = 0.01), and urban light and urban noise together raised call complexity by 17.2% (more chucks) during the rival playback (interaction p = 0.02, above the 14.0% expected under additivity). Sensory treatment did not affect total number of calls, call rate or call overlap (all p > 0.08), and no other treatment effects on call complexity were found during chorus playback or silence (all p > 0.35).

quote: Anthropogenic noise most likely influences signaling via the mechanism of masking, although we did not find a significant impact of noise exposure when tested in isolation.
note: Behavioural null, protocol-specific (noise tested in isolation, against forest-noise playback control, wild-caught lab-held males). The paper's Abstract states that exposure to ALAN alone increased call amplitude and that ALAN and noise combined interacted to give higher call complexity and amplitude; these light-involving results are not filed here.
